claim: A wealth of Drosophila neuroscience data have become available in recent years including cell type and connectome/synaptome datasets for both the larva and adult fly.
source: In recent years, a wealth of Drosophila neuroscience data have become available including cell type and connectome/synaptome datasets for both the larva and adult fly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple datasets mentioned throughout the manuscript (Chiang et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Takemura et al., 2017a; Scheffer et al., 2020).

claim: FlyBrainLab is an open-source computing platform that integrates 3D exploration and visualization of diverse datasets with interactive exploration of the functional logic of modeled executable brain circuits.
source: To facilitate integration across data modalities and to accelerate the understanding of the functional logic of the fruit fly brain, we have developed FlyBrainLab, a unique open-source computing platform that integrates 3D exploration and visualization of diverse datasets with interactive exploration of the functional logic of modeled executable brain circuits.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the developed platform, supported by the description of the system architecture and capabilities throughout the manuscript.

claim: FlyBrainLab's User Interface, Utilities Libraries and Circuit Libraries bring together neuroanatomical, neurogenetic and electrophysiological datasets with computational models.
source: FlyBrainLab's User Interface, Utilities Libraries and Circuit Libraries bring together neuroanatomical, neurogenetic and electrophysiological datasets with computational models of different researchers for validation and comparison within the same platform.
evidence: This claim is supported by the detailed descriptions of these components in the Materials and methods section and the use cases presented.

claim: FlyBrainLab provides libraries for molecular transduction arising in sensory coding in vision/olfaction.
source: Seeking to transcend the limitations of the connectome/synaptome, FlyBrainLab also provides libraries for molecular transduction arising in sensory coding in vision/olfaction.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the EOScircuits Library and the olfactory transduction models in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The era of connectomics/synaptomics has highlighted the dearth of computational tools with the speed and scale that can be effectively deployed to uncover the functional logic of fly brain circuits.
source: The era of connectomics/synaptomics ushered in the advent of large-scale availability of highly complex fruit fly brain data (Chiang et al., 2011; Berck et al., 2016; Takemura et al., 2017a; Scheffer et al., 2020), while simultaneously highlighting the dearth of computational tools with the speed and scale that can be effectively deployed to uncover the functional logic of fly brain circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a motivation for the development of FlyBrainLab.

claim: Automation tools introduced in computational genomics in the early 2000's significantly accelerated the pace of gene discovery from large amounts of genomic data.
source: In the early 2000's, automation tools introduced in computational genomics significantly accelerated the pace of gene discovery from the large amounts of genomic data.
evidence: This is a historical claim used as an analogy, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: FlyBrainLab is designed with three main capabilities: 3D exploration and visualization of fruit fly brain data, creation of executable circuits directly from the explored data, and interactive exploration of the functional logic of the executable circuits.
source: It is designed with three main capabilities in mind: (1) 3D exploration and visualization of fruit fly brain data, (2) creation of executable circuits directly from the explored and visualized fly brain data in step (1), and (3) interactive exploration of the functional logic of the executable circuits devised in step (2) (see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and illustrated in Figure 1, which shows the workflow of the platform.

claim: FlyBrainLab integrates fly brain data in the NeuroArch Database and provides circuit execution with the Neurokernel Execution Engine.
source: To achieve tight integration of the three main capabilities sketched in Figure 1 into a single working environment, FlyBrainLab integrates fly brain data in the NeuroArch Database (Givon et al., 2015) and provides circuit execution with the Neurokernel Execution Engine (Givon and Lazar, 2016) (see Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the underlying technologies and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: The NeuroArch Database stores neuroanatomy datasets from FlyCircuit, Larva L1EM, the Medulla 7 Column and Hemibrain.
source: The NeuroArch Database stores neuroanatomy datasets provided by for example, FlyCircuit (Chiang et al., 2011), Larva L1EM (Ohyama et al., 2015), the Medulla 7 Column (Takemura et al., 2017a) and Hemibrain (Scheffer et al., 2020), genetics datasets published by for example, FlightLight (Jenett et al., 2012) and FlyCircuit (Chiang et al., 2011), and neurophysiology datasets including the DoOR (Münch and Galizia, 2016) and our own in vivo recordings (Lazar and Yeh, 2020; Kim et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the original datasets.

claim: The Neurokernel Execution Engine supports the execution of fruit fly brain circuits on GPUs.
source: The Neurokernel Execution Engine (see Figure 2a) supports the execution of fruit fly brain circuits on GPUs.
evidence: This is a technical capability claim supported by reference to the execution engine and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: NeuroMynerva exhibits an integrated 3D graphics user interface and provides the user a unified view of data integration and computation.
source: Finally, the NeuroMynerva front-end exhibits an integrated 3D graphics user interface (GUI) and provides the user a unified view of data integration and computation (see Figure 2a (top) and Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the visual evidence in Figure 2a and 2b showing the user interface.

claim: The NeuroNLP window supports visual exploration of fly brain data including neuron morphology, synaptome, and connectome from all available data sources stored in the NeuroArch Database.
source: First, the 3D GUI, called the NeuroNLP window (see Figure 2b, top middle-left), supports the visual exploration of fly brain data, including neuron morphology, synaptome, and connectome from all available data sources, stored in the NeuroArch Database (Givon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description and visual evidence in Figure 2b.

claim: A layperson can perform sophisticated database queries with only knowledge of fly brain neuroanatomy using plain English queries in NeuroNLP.
source: With plain English queries (see Figure 2b, top middle-left), a layperson can perform sophisticated database queries with only knowledge of fly brain neuroanatomy (Ukani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the NeuroNLP publication and demonstrated in the use cases.

claim: The NeuroGFX window enables the interactive exploration of executable circuits stored in the NeuroArch Database.
source: Second, the circuit diagram GUI, called the NeuroGFX window (see Figure 2b, top middle-right) enables the interactive exploration of executable circuits stored in the NeuroArch Database.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description and visual evidence in Figure 2b.

claim: NeuroMynerva supports the interaction and interoperability between the biological circuit built for morphological visualization and the executable circuit represented as an interactive circuit diagram.
source: By retrieving tightly integrated biological data and executable circuit models from the NeuroArch Database, NeuroMynerva supports the interaction and interoperability between the biological circuit (or pathway for short) built for morphological visualization and the executable circuit created and represented as an interactive circuit diagram, and allows them to build on each other.
evidence: This claim describes a key capability of the platform, supported by the architectural description.

claim: The GUIs can operate in tandem with command execution in Jupyter notebooks.
source: Third, the GUIs can operate in tandem with command execution in Jupyter notebooks (see also Figure 2b, bottom center).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description and visual evidence in Figure 2b.

claim: Fly brain pathways and circuit diagrams can be equivalently processed using API calls from Python, ensuring reproducibility of the exploration of similar datasets with minimal modifications.
source: Consequently, fly brain pathways and circuit diagrams can be equivalently processed using API calls from Python, thereby ensuring the reproducibility of the exploration of similar datasets with minimal modifications.
evidence: This claim describes a technical capability that supports reproducibility.

claim: The Neurokernel Execution Engine provides circuit execution on multiple computing nodes/GPUs.
source: The Neurokernel Execution Engine (Givon and Lazar, 2016) provides circuit execution on multiple computing nodes/GPUs.
evidence: This is a technical capability claim supported by citation to the Neurokernel publication.

claim: The tight integration between NeuroArch and Neurokernel allows the execution engine to fetch executable circuits directly from the NeuroArch Database.
source: The tight integration in the database also allows the execution engine to fetch executable circuits directly from the NeuroArch Database.
evidence: This describes an architectural feature of the platform.

claim: The motion detection pathway in the fruit fly Medulla has been, in part, mapped out thanks to the Medulla 7 Column dataset.
source: The motion detection pathway in the fruit fly Medulla has been, in part, mapped out thanks to the Medulla 7 Column dataset (Takemura et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Medulla 7 Column dataset publication.

claim: Much research has focused on the direct, feedforward pathway feeding into the motion sensitive T4 neurons.
source: While much research has focussed on the direct, feedforward pathway feeding into the motion sensitive T4 neurons (Takemura et al., 2017b; Haag et al., 2017), the contribution of the feedback pathways and the neighboring columnar neurons to the motion detection circuit has largely been ignored.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on T4 neurons.

claim: The contribution of the feedback pathways and the neighboring columnar neurons to the motion detection circuit has largely been ignored.
source: While much research has focussed on the direct, feedforward pathway feeding into the motion sensitive T4 neurons (Takemura et al., 2017b; Haag et al., 2017), the contribution of the feedback pathways and the neighboring columnar neurons to the motion detection circuit has largely been ignored.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature identified by the authors.

claim: T4a neurons are sensitive to front-to-back-motion.
source: Starting from a T4a neuron in the 'home' column that is sensitive to front-to-back-motion (Maisak et al., 2013 'show T4a in column home'; 'color lime'), we queried its presynaptic neurons ('add presynaptic neurons'; 'color gray') as well as their presynaptic neurons that are non-columnar, in particular, the Dm and Pm cells (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989) ('add presynaptic $Dm$ neurons with at least five synapses'; 'color cyan'; 'add presynaptic $Pm$ neurons with at least five synapses'; 'color yellow').
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maisak et al., 2013.

claim: The mushroom body has been known to be an associative olfactory memory center.
source: The mushroom body (MB) has been known to be an associative olfactory memory center (Modi et al., 2020), whereas the fan-shaped body (FB) shown to be involved in visual pattern memory (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Modi et al., 2020.

claim: The fan-shaped body has been shown to be involved in visual pattern memory.
source: The mushroom body (MB) has been known to be an associative olfactory memory center (Modi et al., 2020), whereas the fan-shaped body (FB) shown to be involved in visual pattern memory (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2006.

claim: The Kenyon cells in the MB receive visual inputs.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the Kenyon cells in the MB also receive visual inputs (Li et al., 2020a), and that the MB and FB are interconnected (Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2020a.

claim: The MB and FB are interconnected.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the Kenyon cells in the MB also receive visual inputs (Li et al., 2020a), and that the MB and FB are interconnected (Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2020b.

claim: The Louvain algorithm applied to all neurons in the Hemibrain dataset shows eight groups of densely connected neurons.
source: By invoking the NeuroGraph Library on the Hemibrain dataset (see Appendix 2), we extracted eight densely connected neuron groups, as shown in Figure 4a.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Six of the eight densely connected groups were assigned to known brain regions/neuropils including the AL, the MB, the LH, the CX, the AVLP, and the SP.
source: We then visualized subsets of neurons pseudocolored by group membership as shown in Figure 4b and assigned six of the eight groups to several known brain regions/neuropils. These neuropils include the AL, the MB, the lateral horn (LH), the central complex (CX), the anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum (AVLP), and the superior protocerebrum (SP).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis and visualization in Figure 4b.

claim: The circuit connecting the ellipsoid body and the protocerebral bridge in the CX has been shown to exhibit ring attractor dynamics.
source: The circuit connecting the ellipsoid body (EB) and the protocerebral bridge (PB) in the CX has been shown to exhibit ring attractor dynamics (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Skaggs et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on ring attractor dynamics.

claim: Model A provides the most complete interactive CX circuit, including the core subcircuits for characterizing the PB-EB interaction with the EB-LAL-PB, PB-EB-LAL, PB-EB-NO, PB local, and EB ring neurons.
source: Here, model A provides the most complete interactive CX circuit, including the core subcircuits for characterizing the PB-EB interaction with the EB-LAL-PB, PB-EB-LAL, PB-EB-NO, PB local, and EB ring neurons (see Materials and methods, Use Case 4, and Givon et al., 2017 for commonly used synonyms).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of Model A and citation to Givon et al., 2017.

claim: No ring neurons are modeled in model B.
source: While no ring neurons are modeled in model B, PB local neurons are omitted in model C.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composition of Model B.

claim: PB local neurons are omitted in model C.
source: While no ring neurons are modeled in model B, PB local neurons are omitted in model C.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composition of Model C.

claim: All three CX models exhibited a single-bump response tracking the position of the moving bar.
source: All three models exhibited a single-bump (slightly delayed) response tracking the position of the moving bar.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 6 (a4, b4, c4).

claim: For models A and B, the bumps shifted to track the location of the static bar after the moving bar disappeared, whereas the bump in model C persisted in the same position where the moving bar disappeared.
source: After 30 s, the moving bar disappeared and models A and B shifted to track the location of the static bar, whereas the bump in model C persisted in the same position where the moving bar disappeared.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 6 (a4, b4, c4).

claim: For models B and C but not for model A, the bumps persisted after the removal of the visual stimulus.
source: Furthermore, for models B and C but not for model A, the bumps persisted after the removal of the visual stimulus (after 33 s), as previously observed in vivo (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results and citations to in vivo observations.

claim: To achieve the ring attractor dynamics, it is critical to include global inhibitory neurons, for example, PB local neurons in models A and B, and ring neurons in models A and C.
source: By comparing these circuit models, we notice that, to achieve the ring attractor dynamics, it is critical to include global inhibitory neurons, for example, PB local neurons in models A and B, and ring neurons in models A and C.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from comparing the three models.

claim: To achieve the ring attractor dynamics characterized by a single bump response to multiple bars and persistent bump activity after the removal of the vertical bar, model C only required three out of the five core neuron types, whereas model B requires all four neuron types included.
source: However, to achieve the ring attractor dynamics characterized by a single bump response to multiple bars and persistent bump activity after the removal of the vertical bar, model C only required three out of the five core neuron types (see Materials and methods, Use Case 4), whereas model B requires all four neuron types included.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from comparing the circuit models.

claim: The Hemibrain dataset reveals additional connectivity details between OSNs, PNs, and LNs compared with the antennal lobe data in the FlyCircuit dataset.
source: Compared with the antennal lobe data in the FlyCircuit dataset, the Hemibrain dataset reveals additional connectivity details between OSNs, PNs, and LNs that we took into account when modeling the antennal lobe circuit (see Materials and methods, Use Case 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of the two datasets shown in Figure 7.

claim: A prediction made by the antenna and antennal lobe circuit using the FlyCircuit data is that the PN activity, bundled according to the source glomerulus, is proportional to the vector characterizing the affinity of the odorant-receptor pairs.
source: A prediction (Lazar and Yeh, 2019; Lazar et al., 2020a) made by the antenna and antennal lobe circuit shown in Figure 7b (left) using the FlyCircuit data has been that the PN activity, bundled according to the source glomerulus, is proportional to the vector characterizing the affinity of the odorant-receptor pairs (Figure 7c, left column).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and the data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The complex connectivity between OSNs, LNs, and PNs revealed by the Hemibrain dataset suggests that the adult antennal lobe circuit encodes additional odorant representation features.
source: The complex connectivity between OSNs, LNs, and PNs revealed by the Hemibrain dataset suggests that the adult antennal lobe circuit encodes additional odorant representation features (Scheffer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed connectivity patterns and supported by citation.

claim: The larval model includes fewer number of OSNs, PNs, and LNs in Antenna and Antennal Lobe circuit compared to the adult model.
source: In particular, the larval model includes fewer number of OSNs, PNs, and LNs in Antenna and Antennal Lobe circuit as shown in Figure 8b right.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8b and Table 1.

claim: There is a stark contrast in odorant representation at all layers of the circuit between adult and larva.
source: Visualized in juxtaposition alongside the corresponding affinity vectors, we observe a stark contrast in odorant representation at all layers of the circuit between adult and larva, raising the question of how downstream circuits can process differently represented odorant identities and instruct similar olfactory behavior across development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 8c.

claim: A number of simulation engines have been developed, including NEURON, NEST, Brian, Nengo, Neurokernel, DynaSim, MOOSE, ARBOR, and The Virtual Brain.
source: A number of simulation engines have been developed, including general simulators such as NEURON (Hines and Carnevale, 1997), NEST (Gewaltig and Diesmann, 2007), Brian (Stimberg et al., 2019), Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014), Neurokernel (Givon and Lazar, 2016), DynaSim (Sherfey et al., 2018), and the ones that specialize in multi-scale simulation, for example MOOSE (Ray and Bhalla, 2008), in compartmental models, for example ARBOR (Akar et al., 2019), and in fMRI-scale simulation for example The Virtual Brain (Sanz Leon et al., 2013; Melozzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to simulation engines.

claim: Tools like BMTK and NetPyNE facilitate the creation of large-scale neural networks.
source: Other tools improve the accessibility to these simulators by (i) facilitating the creation of large-scale neural networks, for example BMTK (Dai et al., 2020a) and NetPyNE (Dura-Bernal et al., 2019), and by (ii) providing a common interface, simplifying the simulation workflow and streamlining parallelization of simulation, for example PyNN (Davison et al., 2008), Arachne (Aleksin et al., 2017), and NeuroManager (Stockton and Santamaria, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to these tools.

claim: A number of model specification standards have been developed including MorphML, NeuroML, SpineML, and SONATA.
source: To facilitate access and exchange of neurobiological data worldwide, a number of model specification standards have been worked upon in parallel including MorphML (Crook et al., 2007), NeuroML (Gleeson et al., 2010), SpineML (Tomkins et al., 2016), and SONATA (Dai et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to these standards.

claim: It takes a substantial amount of manual effort to build executable circuits from real data provided by model databases such as ModelDB/NeuronDB and NeuroArch.
source: Even with the help of these computational tools, it still takes a substantial amount of manual effort to build executable circuits from real data provided, for example, by model databases such as ModelDB/NeuronDB (Hines et al., 2004) and NeuroArch (Givon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim represents a challenge in the field identified by the authors.

claim: With the ever expanding size of the fruit fly brain datasets, it has become more difficult to meet the demand of creating executable circuits that can be evaluated with different datasets.
source: Moreover, with the ever expanding size of the fruit fly brain datasets, it has become more difficult to meet the demand of creating executable circuits that can be evaluated with different datasets.
evidence: This claim represents a challenge in the field identified by the authors.

claim: Comparisons of circuit models are rarely available in the computational neuroscience literature.
source: In addition, with very few exceptions, comparisons of circuit models, a standard process in the computer science community, are rarely available in the computational neuroscience literature.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature identified by the authors.

claim: A number of tools have been developed to provide interactive, web-based interfaces for exploring, visualizing and analyzing fruit fly brain and ventral nerve cord datasets, including FlyCircuit, FFBO/NeuroNLP, Virtual Fly Brain, neuPrintExplorer, FlyWire, and CATMAID.
source: A number of tools have been developed to provide interactive, web-based interfaces for exploring, visualizing and analyzing fruit fly brain and ventral nerve cord datasets, for both the adult (Chiang et al., 2011; Scheffer et al., 2020) and the larva (Ohyama et al., 2015). These include the FlyCircuit (Chiang et al., 2011), the Fruit Fly Brain Observatory (FFBO/NeuroNLP) (Ukani et al., 2019), Virtual Fly Brain (Milyaev et al., 2012), neuPrintExplorer (Clements et al., 2020), FlyWire (Dorkenwald et al., 2020), and CATMAID (Saalfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to visualization tools.

claim: Recent efforts have started to bridge the gap between neurobiological data and computational modeling including Geppetto, OpenWorm, Open Source Brain, and the Brain Simulation Platform of the Human Brain Project.
source: While these tools have significantly improved the access to and exploration of brain data a number of recent efforts started to bridge the gap between neurobiological data and computational modeling including the Geppetto (Cantarelli et al., 2018), the OpenWorm (Szigeti et al., 2014) and the Open Source Brain (Gleeson et al., 2019) initiatives and the Brain Simulation Platform of the Human Brain Project (Einevoll et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to these initiatives.

claim: Without information linking circuit activity/computation to the structure of the underlying neuronal circuits, understanding the function of brain circuits remains elusive.
source: However, without information linking circuit activity/computation to the structure of the underlying neuronal circuits, understanding the function of brain circuits remains elusive.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenge in neuroscience.

claim: Lacking a systematic method of automating the process of creating and exploring the function of executable circuits at the brain or system scale levels hinders the application of these tools when composing more complex circuits.
source: Lacking a systematic method of automating the process of creating and exploring the function of executable circuits at the brain or system scale levels hinders the application of these tools when composing more complex circuits.
evidence: This claim represents a limitation of existing tools identified by the authors.

claim: Visualization of a biological circuit alone provides little insights into the function of the circuit.
source: Similarly, visualization of a biological circuit alone, while powerful and intuitive for building a neural circuit, provides little insights into the function of the circuit.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of visualization alone.

claim: While simulations can be done without a circuit diagram, understanding how an executable circuit leads to its function remains elusive.
source: While simulations can be done without a circuit diagram, understanding how an executable circuit leads to its function remains elusive.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenge in understanding circuit function.

claim: Creating circuit simulations from visualized data remains a major challenge and requires extraordinary effort in practice as demonstrated by the Allen Brain Observatory.
source: Creating circuit simulations from visualized data remains a major challenge and requires extraordinary effort in practice as amply demonstrated by the Allen Brain Observatory (de Vries et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Allen Brain Observatory.

claim: FlyBrainLab is uniquely positioned to accelerate the discovery of the functional logic of the Drosophila brain.
source: FlyBrainLab is uniquely positioned to accelerate the discovery of the functional logic of the Drosophila brain.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the platform's capabilities.

claim: FlyBrainLab's interactive architecture seamlessly integrates and brings together computational models with neuroanatomical, neurogenetic, and neurophysiological data.
source: Its interactive architecture seamlessly integrates and brings together computational models with neuroanatomical, neurogenetic, and neurophysiological data, changing the organization of fruit fly brain data from a group of independently created datasets, arrays, and tables, into a well-structured data and executable circuit repository, with a simple API for accessing data in different datasets.
evidence: This claim describes a key feature of the platform.

claim: Current data integration extensively focuses on connectomics/synaptomics datasets that strongly inform the construction of executable circuit models.
source: Current data integration extensively focuses on connectomics/synaptomics datasets that, as demonstrated, strongly inform the construction of executable circuit models.
evidence: This claim describes the current focus of the platform.

claim: The FlyBrainLab UI supports a highly intuitive and automated workflow that streamlines the 3D exploration and visualization of fly brain circuits, and the interactive exploration of the functional logic of executable circuits created directly from the analyzed fly brain data.
source: As detailed here, the FlyBrainLab UI supports a highly intuitive and automated workflow that streamlines the 3D exploration and visualization of fly brain circuits, and the interactive exploration of the functional logic of executable circuits created directly from the analyzed fly brain data.
evidence: This claim summarizes the capabilities of the UI.

claim: Speeding up the process of creating interactive executable circuit diagrams can substantially reduce the exploratory development cycle.
source: In conjunction with the capability of visually constructing circuits, speeding up the process of creating interactive executable circuit diagrams can substantially reduce the exploratory development cycle.
evidence: This is a claim about the benefit of the platform's capabilities.

claim: The FlyBrainLab Utility and Circuit Libraries accelerate the creation of models of executable circuits.
source: The FlyBrainLab Utility and Circuit Libraries accelerate the creation of models of executable circuits.
evidence: This is a claim about the function of the libraries.

claim: The Utility Libraries help untangle the graph structure of neural circuits from raw connectome and synaptome data.
source: The Utility Libraries (detailed in the Appendix 2) help untangle the graph structure of neural circuits from raw connectome and synaptome data.
evidence: This is a claim about the function of the Utility Libraries.

claim: The Circuit Libraries facilitate the exploration of neural circuits of the neuropils of the central complex and the development and implementation of models of the adult and larva fruit fly early olfactory system.
source: The Circuit Libraries (detailed in the Appendix 3) facilitate the exploration of neural circuits of the neuropils of the central complex and, the development and implementation of models of the adult and larva fruit fly early olfactory system.
evidence: This is a claim about the function of the Circuit Libraries.

claim: FlyBrainLab is providing Circuit Libraries for molecular transduction in sensory coding, including models of sensory transduction and neuron activity data.
source: Importantly, to transcend the limitations of the connectome, FlyBrainLab is providing Circuit Libraries for molecular transduction in sensory coding (detailed in the Appendix 3), including models of sensory transduction and neuron activity data (Lazar et al., 2015a; Lazar et al., 2015b; Lazar and Yeh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the models and data.

claim: These libraries serve as entry points for discovery of circuit function in the sensory systems of the fruit fly.
source: These libraries serve as entry points for discovery of circuit function in the sensory systems of the fruit fly (Lazar and Yeh, 2019; Lazar et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The libraries enable the biological validation of developed executable circuits within the same platform.
source: They also enable the biological validation of developed executable circuits within the same platform.
evidence: This is a claim about the capability of the libraries.

claim: The modular software architecture underlying FlyBrainLab provides substantial flexibility and scalability for the study of the larva and adult fruit fly brain.
source: The modular software architecture underlying FlyBrainLab provides substantial flexibility and scalability for the study of the larva and adult fruit fly brain.
evidence: This is a claim about the architecture of the platform.

claim: As more data becomes available, the entire central nervous system of the fruit fly can be readily explored with FlyBrainLab.
source: As more data becomes available, we envision that the entire central nervous system of the fruit fly can be readily explored with FlyBrainLab.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future capabilities.

claim: The core of the software and the workflow enabled by FlyBrainLab can be adapted in the near term to other model organisms including the zebrafish and bee.
source: Furthermore, the core of the software and the workflow enabled by the FlyBrainLab for accelerating discovery of Drosophila brain functions can be adapted in the near term to other model organisms including the zebrafish and bee.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications.

claim: For the FlyCircuit dataset version 1.2, all 22,828 female Drosophila neurons were loaded, including their morphology, putative neurotransmitter type, and other available metadata.
source: For the FlyCircuit dataset (Chiang et al., 2011) version 1.2, all 22,828 female Drosophila neurons were loaded, including their morphology, putative neurotransmitter type, and other available metadata.
evidence: This is a factual claim about the data loading process.

claim: Connectivity between neurons in the FlyCircuit dataset was inferred according to Huang et al., 2018 and loaded as a different, inferred class of synapses, totaling 4,538,280 connections between pairs of neurons.
source: Connectivity between neurons was inferred according to Huang et al., 2018 and loaded as a different, inferred class of synapses, totaling 4,538,280 connections between pairs of neurons.
evidence: This is a factual claim about the data loading process, supported by citation.

claim: For the Hemibrain dataset release 1.0.1, a total of 24,770 neurons were included that were designated in the Neuprint database as 'Traced', 'Roughly Traced', as well as the neurons that were assigned a name or a cell type.
source: It included a total of 24,770 neurons that were designated in the Neuprint database as 'Traced', 'Roughly Traced', as well as the neurons that were assigned a name or a cell type.
evidence: This is a factual claim about the data loading process.

claim: A total of 3,604,708 connections between pairs of neurons were loaded from the Hemibrain dataset release 1.0.1, and included the positions of 14,318,675 synapses.
source: A total of 3,604,708 connections between pairs of neurons were loaded, and included the positions of 14,318,675 synapses.
evidence: This is a factual claim about the data loading process.

claim: For the Larva L1EM dataset, a total of 1,051 neurons characterized by their morphology and metadata were loaded.
source: For the Larva L1EM dataset (Ohyama et al., 2015), a total of 1,051 neurons characterized by their morphology and metadata were loaded from the publicly served database server at https://l1em.catmaid.virtualflybrain.org.
evidence: This is a factual claim about the data loading process.

claim: A total of 30,350 connections between pairs of neurons were loaded from the Larva L1EM dataset, including the position of 121,112 synapses.
source: A total of 30,350 connections between pairs of neurons were loaded, including the position of 121,112 synapses.
evidence: This is a factual claim about the data loading process.

claim: For the Medulla 7 Column dataset, a total of 2365 neurons, 42,279 connections between pairs of neurons, and the positions of 130,203 synapses were loaded.
source: A total of 2365 neurons, 42,279 connections between pairs of neurons, and the positions of 130,203 synapses were loaded.
evidence: This is a factual claim about the data loading process.
